opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I first started working on robotics, embodied intelligence wasn't a hot topic at all. It was a fairly niche corner of research. Most of the excitement in AI was around vision benchmarks, then language models. Robotics was seen as slow, expensive, and hard to scale. You'd spend months getting a robot arm to reliably grasp a handful of objects in a lab, and the moment you changed the lighting or the table, things fell apart.

So the surge we're seeing now didn't come out of nowhere. I think a few things converged.

The first is large models. When people saw what language and multimodal models could do, they realized we finally had something like a general "brain" for understanding instructions, reasoning about scenes, and planning at a high level. The natural next question was: if AI can understand the world this well, why can't it act in it? That question pushed a lot of attention, talent, and capital toward embodiment.

The second is hardware maturity, especially in China. Supply chains for motors, reducers, sensors, and batteries have become much cheaper and more capable. Building a reasonably good humanoid or mobile manipulator is no longer something only a handful of labs in the world can do.

The third, and to me the most important, is that people are beginning to take the data problem seriously. Language models had the internet. Robots have no internet of physical interaction. Teleoperation data is expensive and hard to scale. So from early on I've believed that synthetic data and simulation, generating large amounts of physically plausible interaction data, is key to generalization. When you can train a grasping or manipulation policy mostly in simulation and have it transfer zero-shot to the real world across many objects and scenes, that's when you start to feel this could actually scale.

That said, I try to stay a bit sober about the hype. There's a gap between impressive demos and robots doing useful, reliable work every day in factories, stores, or homes. Demos can be cherry-picked; real deployment can't. A lot of the hard problems, like dexterous manipulation, long-horizon tasks, and robustness to the messiness of the real world, are still very much open.

So my view is that the surge is justified in direction but probably ahead of reality in timing. It's a genuinely historic opportunity. For the first time, the algorithms, the hardware, and the data approaches are all reaching a usable level together. But the field will be won by teams that patiently solve generalization and deliver real value in concrete scenarios, not by whoever has the flashiest video.

r001.rationale: The response says the field was once niche and that interest has surged, but it does not describe this surge as increased recognition of people already working in the field.

r002.rationale: It mentions hardware maturity, especially in China, but gives no comparison of when embodied intelligence gained traction in the United States versus mainland China.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. When I first entered the field, this was still a very niche thing. Around 2017, 2018, when I was doing my PhD at Stanford, "embodied intelligence" wasn't even a phrase most people used. We just said robotics, or robot learning, and most of my colleagues in computer vision thought of it as a somewhat marginal direction. You'd train a model on ImageNet, and that was mainstream. Working on a robot arm that could grasp objects was slow, expensive, and the results were hard to publish.

So I think the surge we're seeing now comes from three things coming together.

The first is that perception finally got good enough. For a long time the bottleneck wasn't the robot, it was that the robot couldn't really understand what it was looking at. My own work on 6D pose estimation and category-level object understanding came from this frustration. If you can't tell where a cup is and how it's oriented, you can't grasp it, no matter how good your controller is. Over the past few years, 3D vision and foundation models have closed a big part of that gap.

The second is the large language model moment. ChatGPT changed how people think about what "intelligence" means. Suddenly there's a system that can reason in language, and the obvious next question everyone asks is: why can't it act in the physical world? That question pulled in enormous attention and capital that previously had no reason to look at robotics.

The third is more structural. China has the most complete manufacturing supply chain for hardware in the world. Motors, reducers, sensors, battery packs. So when the software side started looking promising, the cost of building a humanoid or a dexterous hand dropped very quickly here. That's why you see so many Chinese startups in this space right now.

But I'd also say, from the inside, the heat is a bit ahead of the technology. Language models learned from the entire internet. Robots don't have an internet of physical interaction data. The core problem I spend most of my time on now is exactly this: how do you get enough data, through simulation, synthetic generation, and real-world collection, to make generalizable manipulation actually work? That's not solved yet. So I'm very optimistic about the direction, but I think people should be patient about the timeline.

r001.rationale: The response says the field was niche and now attracts attention, but attributes the surge to better perception, the LLM moment, and China’s hardware supply chain. It does not frame the surge as increased recognition of people already working in the field.

r002.rationale: The response mentions the speaker’s Stanford PhD period and current Chinese startups, but does not state that embodied intelligence gained traction earlier in the United States than in mainland China.

astra-6.text:
I think the recent interest reflects a convergence of two ambitions: making AI more capable and making robots more useful. Embodied intelligence sits at that intersection. It asks whether intelligence can go beyond processing information and actually perceive, act, and learn through interaction with the physical world.

What makes that compelling is also what makes it difficult. A robot has to close the loop: it observes something, takes an action, and deals with the consequences. If its understanding is wrong, the next observation will reveal that. And the world is full of variation—objects move, lighting changes, and a task that looks simple can require very precise control.

So I would distinguish the surge of interest from the underlying challenge. More attention creates opportunities to bring different approaches together, but it doesn’t make those physical problems disappear. For me, the important question is whether we can turn promising demonstrations into capabilities that work reliably across different situations. That’s where the excitement becomes meaningful progress.

r001.rationale: The response describes interest as a convergence of ambitions, but does not frame it as increased recognition of people already working in the field.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare when embodied intelligence gained traction in the United States and mainland China.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the excitement comes from the possibility of connecting intelligence with action. A system can describe a task very convincingly, but putting it in the physical world raises a different set of questions: Can it perceive what matters, decide what to do, and adapt when the result is different from what it expected?

To me, that is what makes embodied intelligence so compelling. Perception, learning, and control have to work together, and the environment gives you very concrete feedback. You either grasp the object successfully or you don’t.

I would also distinguish the surge of interest from the maturity of the technology. There is a lot of enthusiasm about general-purpose robots, but making a system reliable across unfamiliar objects, tasks, and environments remains difficult. The excitement is valuable if it brings more people into those underlying problems and sustains the patient work needed to solve them.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the excitement to connecting intelligence with physical action and the challenges of reliable robots; it does not frame the surge as recognition of people already working in the field.

r002.rationale: The response gives no comparison of when embodied intelligence gained traction in the United States versus mainland China.
